variants.name: Phantom state parameter + constrained extensions
variants.implementation_notes: Swift generics carry a phantom state parameter (struct CheckoutForm<State>) and constrained extensions add state-specific methods (extension CheckoutForm where State == Incomplete), so an illegal step is simply a missing member; empty enums are the conventional zero-sized state markers. Values are copyable by default, which loses the consume half of the pattern, so Swift 5.9 added noncopyable types (~Copyable) together with consuming methods to make a transition invalidate its source. The one-type-per-state form - an enum with associated values plus an exhaustive switch - remains the simpler choice when states carry different data.
pitfalls: Value semantics copy the state: without ~Copyable a pre-transition copy can be advanced again, duplicating the workflow's effects.
Erasing the phantom parameter through Any or a protocol existential removes the state-specific extensions, leaving only the shared API.
The strongest form is constrained: noncopyable types cannot be used as generic parameters or stored in arrays and optionals today, so consuming transitions work only for concrete state types.

variants.name: Noncopyable states with consuming transitions (Swift 5.9)
variants.implementation_notes: Swift 5.9's noncopyable structs plus consuming methods make the transition linear: the method takes the value and the source becomes statically invalid afterwards, which matches Rust's ownership half. Use it for single-owner, mission-critical workflows where duplicating a state would be a safety bug; it is limited to concrete noncopyable types and adding ~Copyable to an existing type is an ABI change.
pitfalls: Adding ~Copyable to an existing public type changes its ABI and how callers may use it.
Noncopyable types cannot be generic parameters, array elements or optional payloads today, so keep them at the boundary of the workflow.
